title: Study Abroad Report: National Taiwan University
paragraphs: I was allowed to study abroad and do clerkships for a total of two months at National Taiwan University in Taiwan in four clinical departments: gastroenterology, endocrinology, family medicine and medical oncology. This year I was the only person who went from Nagoya University to National Taiwan University. For that reason I was full of anxiety before departure, but I was able to spend two enjoyable months.

National Taiwan University is one of the former imperial universities established before the war, founded in 1928, before Nagoya University was established. As at Nagoya University, the campus of the medical school and the campuses of other faculties are separate, and the medical school campus was located about a 10-minute walk from Taipei Main Station, the main station. First, what surprised me on my first visit was the size of the hospital. National Taiwan University has four ward buildings, A, B, C and D, each about 17 floors. The outpatient building is separate and was a hospital from the period of Japanese rule, renovated and used as it is. In addition, the pediatrics building is set up individually, and a building consolidating the minor departments was to be built next year. I wondered whether it was too big even for the top university in Taiwan, but the reason lay in the healthcare system. Taiwan has a universal health insurance system like Japan, but there is no designated medical care fee, so people can visit a university hospital for a first consultation at very low cost. For that reason, patients flock to National Taiwan University Hospital, the best hospital in Taiwan, and that is why the hospital has become so large. Not only the size of the hospital but also the charts were very different. A system equivalent to what is called the "My Number insurance card" in Japan is firmly widespread, and individuals' image data are managed centrally on the cloud. As a result, there is no need to transfer image data to other hospitals, and referrals were carried out smoothly.

I was allowed to observe gastroenterology, endocrinology, family medicine and medical oncology for two weeks each. In gastroenterology, my impression was that it is not much different from Japan, for example in referring to Japanese endoscopy guidelines. It was basically in the form of a face-to-face version of PBL, deepening understanding while discussing with the professor the patients admitted that week. I was allowed to observe a liver biopsy, which I had not been able to observe in Japan. In endocrinology, I listened to presentations in the morning and observed thyroid ultrasound in the afternoon. What especially impressed me was that in discussion I learned about surgery for diabetes. In Taiwan it is covered by insurance, and I was told it is actively recommended for patients with a BMI of 37.5 or higher. I could not compare medical oncology because we do not rotate through it in the Nagoya University polyclinic, but my impression was that it is tremendously busy, with each doctor seeing 50 to 60 patients in the outpatient clinic in the morning. The clerkship consisted of attending conferences and observing procedures such as CV port placement. They mainly perform chemotherapy in outpatient and inpatient settings and also conduct clinical trials in cooperation with the adjacent research building. Finally, the department that impressed me most was family medicine. In family medicine there were various clerkship activities, from observing outpatient clinics to accompanying hospice home care. The outpatient clinics were wide-ranging, from a travelers' clinic run on rotation by doctors of the Taiwanese version of the CCD to a geriatric clinic. In hospice home care, I was allowed to accompany two nurses and one doctor and visited the home of a woman in her 90s with end-stage renal failure. In preparation for dying at home, they were issuing a terminal certificate and consulting with the family about the types and amounts of medicines in the future.

First, about food. Taiwanese cuisine is generally lightly seasoned, which suited my taste and I found it very delicious. Food costs were also very reasonable, basically about 70% of Japan's. Next, regarding the climate, since my study abroad was in February and March, it was a little chilly, but not to the extent of needing a coat or knitwear, and it was very comfortable. Finally, about free time locally. I went sightseeing to various places with a Taiwanese friend I had met at a language study abroad in the Philippines, an Australian fellow exchange student, and friends who visited me from Japan. The one that stays most in my memory was climbing a mountain called Yangmingshan with the Australian student. The altitude is only about 1000 m, not that high, but the slope was steep and it was very hard. But the sense of accomplishment after reaching the summit was great and very pleasant.

I was able to meet wonderful doctors, friends and students, and it became a very fruitful experience. I sincerely thank Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and all the members of the International Collaboration Office, the staff of the Academic Affairs Division, and the doctors of National Taiwan University, who supported this valuable experience.
